hero.h1: Somebody else did it, and you arranged it
hero.lede: Not a tense but a shape, and one English uses constantly. You stay the subject — it was your decision and your money — while the hands belong to a hairdresser, a garage or a roofer who never makes it into the sentence at all. The whole trick is where you put the thing.

sections.label: Moon briefing
sections.title: When to use it
sections.lead: The causative is the sentence for work you arrange rather than do. You are still the subject — it is your money and your decision — but the hands belong to somebody you usually do not bother to name.

cards.head: A service you pay for
cards.body: The classic use, and the reason it exists.

cards.head: Work on a house, a car, a tooth
cards.body: Anywhere a professional does the thing to your thing.

cards.head: Get instead of have
cards.body: More informal, and slightly more effort on your part.

cards.head: Something bad that happened to you
cards.body: Here you arranged nothing. This is the other causative.

cards.head: Making somebody do it
cards.body: With a person and no to: this one is about authority.

charts.head: So is this the passive?
charts.note: Half of it is, which is why the causative sits on the descent side of the mountain rather than up with the tenses. The main clause is active — you are the subject and you did the arranging. What follows have is a passive in miniature: my hair cut is my hair [was] cut with the auxiliary squeezed out. Many coursebooks call it the causative passive for exactly that reason.

head: Part of the sentence
Voice
Why
rows: You are the subject and the arranger.
The hair is having it done to it, by somebody unnamed.
The full passive — and it loses you entirely.
The plain active — and now you held the scissors.

charts.example: The causative is the sentence English uses when neither plain voice will do: the passive loses you, the active makes you the barber. This one keeps you responsible and still hands the work to somebody else — which is exactly what happened.

charts.head: The word order is the whole trick
charts.note: The thing comes before the participle, never after it. Put the participle next to have and you have written the present perfect instead, which says something completely different about who did the work.

head: Sentence
Means
Who did it
rows: Present perfect: I did it myself, earlier.
I climbed up and repaired it.

charts.head: It moves through every tense
charts.note: Only have changes. The thing and the participle behind it never move, so once you can hear the order you can build it in any tense on the mountain.

head: Tense
Example
Camp
rows: I have my hair cut every month.
I had my hair cut on Friday.
I'll have my hair cut before the wedding.
I'm having my hair cut at three.

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Almost every error with the causative is one of these three.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: I had cut my hair at the salon.
I had my hair cut at the salon.
The thing goes between had and the participle. Otherwise you cut it yourself.
I had the plumber to look at it.
I had the plumber look at it.
Have + person takes the bare infinitive. Only get takes to.
It is the third form, and for cut that is cut.

charts.note: They are close enough that most of the time either works. Where they differ is in how much effort the sentence implies on your part, and what follows when a person is involved.

head: Question
have
get
rows: Informal, and more common in speech.
Some. You had to persuade or chase.

charts.example: The pair that shows the order: "I had cut my hair" — I stood in front of a mirror with scissors. "I had my hair cut" — I sat in a chair and paid. Three words, same words, and the only difference is where my hair sits.

sections.label: Trail markers
sections.title: Signal words

signals.head: Where you will meet it
items: anything you pay somebody to do

sections.example: A useful habit: if you can put somebody else did it, and I organised it after the sentence and it still makes sense, the causative is the form you want.

diagram.intro: Three boxes and two arrows. You are still the subject on the left, because it was your decision and your money. The thing on the right is what actually changes. The dashed box in the middle is whoever did the work — drawn dashed for the same reason as on the descent, because English lets you leave them out entirely. Click your box or theirs to see it in a sentence.

panels.head: You — the one who arranged it
Them — the one who did it
items: … by a hairdresser on the high street.
… and normally you would not mention them at all.

quiz.prompt: I _____ on Friday. (have / my hair / cut)
quiz.explain: The thing goes between had and the participle. Had cut my hair would mean you did it yourself.

quiz.prompt: We _____ last month. (have / the kitchen / rewire)
quiz.explain: Have + thing + past participle. Rewire / rewired / rewired.

quiz.prompt: I must _____ before the interview. (get / this jacket / clean)
quiz.explain: Get works exactly like have with a thing: get + thing + participle.

quiz.prompt: They _____ outside the station. (have / their car / steal)
quiz.explain: The other causative: something bad happened to you. Steal / stole / stolen.

quiz.prompt: She _____ the bags. (have / the porter / carry)
quiz.explain: Have + person takes the bare infinitive, with no to.

quiz.prompt: I _____ me with the boxes. (get / my brother / help)
quiz.explain: Get + person always takes to. Have never does.

quiz.prompt: I _____ myself, and it was a disaster.
quiz.explain: Myself rules out the causative entirely: you did it.
The causative sits inside any tense: have had + thing + participle.

quiz.prompt: We _____ next week. (have / the roof / repair)
quiz.explain: The continuous of an arrangement: are having + thing + participle.

quiz.prompt: He _____ at the airport. (have / his phone / take)
quiz.explain: Take / took / taken. Nothing was arranged; it happened to him.

quiz.prompt: I _____ before the wedding. (will / have / my suit / press)
She _____ every six weeks. (have / her hair / colour)
quiz.explain: Present simple, third person: has + thing + participle.

quiz.prompt: I _____ the quote by Friday. (get / them / send)

quiz.explain: With no arranger in the sentence, the plain passive does the job.

results: Clean run. The thing goes in the middle, and you know when get needs a to.
Solid progress. Worth another look at the word order before you go on.
Good first attempt. Where the thing sits is the part to read again.
